extracted.intended_audience: inventors, companies, and foreign applicants seeking to file a patent in Brazil (and their counsel or agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step procedural guidance for preparing, filing, prosecuting, and maintaining a patent application before Brazil's National Institute of Industrial Property (INPI), including timelines, translation and fee requirements, examination requests, and maintenance annuities. Focuses on both national and PCT/Paris Convention routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility (substantive requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible for protection, an invention must be new, inventive, and industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although there is no statutory definition of 'invention', the Brazilian Patent Statute provides a list of what does not qualify as one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prior art search before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: First, we recommend conducting a prior art search to determine if your invention qualifies for patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The firm offers to perform this search free of charge; a prior search helps assess patentability and avoid filing for non‑novel or obvious subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay required application fees to INPI
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure to pay the required application fees to INPI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment of application fees is a prerequisite to proceed with filing; failure to pay may prevent acceptance of the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing modes and forms (Paris Convention / PCT national phase)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can file the application under the Paris Convention or as a PCT national phase entry; complete and file the necessary forms online through the INPI portal or in person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate filing route based on priority claims and international strategy; ensure correct selection of national vs. international route at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portuguese translation requirements at filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sure to submit Portuguese translations of the claims and abstract at filing, and the full translation within 60 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims and abstract must be translated immediately at filing; complete specification translation must follow within 60 days to comply with INPI requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application publication timing and early publication option
rubrics_metrics.description: INPI usually publishes the application within six months of the national filing date; you may request early publication by paying an additional fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that examination won’t begin until publication occurs, so early publication can accelerate prosecution if desired and paid for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request examination within 36 months
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 36 months from the international or national filing date, you must request examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to request examination within the 36‑month window can result in abandonment; time counts from the international or national filing date as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to INPI Examination Report (FER) within 90 days
rubrics_metrics.description: INPI will issue an Examination Report (FER) or Office Action outlining objections or requirements. You’ll have 90 days to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare substantive amendments, arguments, or evidence within the 90‑day response period to overcome objections; missing deadlines risks abandonment or adverse decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Allowance — pay grant fee within 60 days
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the INPI issues the Notice of Allowance, applicants must pay the official grant fee within 60 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely payment of the grant fee is required for issuance of the patent; failure to pay within the 60‑day window may forfeit grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annuity (maintenance) payments beginning third year
rubrics_metrics.description: From the third year after filing, and after approval, you must pay annuity fees to maintain the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular annuity payments are required to keep the patent in force; non‑payment leads to lapse. The firm notes annuities are payable after approval/starting from year three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: After grant, the patent remains valid for 20 years from the filing date, provided that annuity fees are paid regularly to maintain its enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 20‑year term counted from filing date; maintenance fees must be kept up to retain enforceability during the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for local legal representation for foreign applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign applicants must appoint a patent attorney or agent registered in Brazil to handle the prosecution process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local representation ensures compliance with INPI formalities and proper communication; nonresidents cannot prosecute without a registered local agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated processing time
rubrics_metrics.description: On average, the patent grant process in Brazil takes about 5 years from the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical timeline cited as around 4 to 5 years, but this may vary depending on complexity and number/length of office actions issued by INPI.

rubrics_metrics.name: International treaty membership implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Brazil is a member of both the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) and the Paris Convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, applicants can file international patent applications through the PCT or claim priority under the Paris Convention when filing in Brazil; choose filing strategy accordingly.
